hook_text: Every wire fights the current a little. In your kettle, that fight is the whole point.
clip_script: Electrons rushing through a wire are like learners racing down a crowded corridor. They keep bumping into things, the atoms of the metal, and slow down. That opposition is resistance, measured in ohms. Copper has very little, which is why it is used for wires. Plastic has so much that almost nothing gets through. More resistance means less current, so add a second bulb in series and both glow dimmer. And every bump turns some electrical energy into heat. Usually that is waste. But inside your kettle, stove, toaster and geyser is a coil of nichrome, a high-resistance wire designed to get very hot without melting. An old light bulb pushes it further: a tungsten wire so hot it glows white. Resistors on circuit boards hold the current back to protect LEDs, and the volume knob on a radio is a resistor you can turn.
visual_style: Animated electrons jostling through a lattice of atoms; a kettle element glowing red; a filament bulb in slow motion; a rheostat slider dimming a bulb.
pacing: Corridor analogy, quick rule, then a tour of hot wires around the kitchen.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and find the resistors in your home.
